title: Childhood in wartime
text:
Childhood in wartime
The war in Ukraine has had a disproportionate impact on the country’s children. In our magazine this week, we revisit families helping young people maintain resilience.
On a walk with a friend along Lake Ontario in Toronto, I shared that our war correspondent, Scott Peterson, had pitched another trip to Ukraine. Scott had visited the country 12 times since Russia’s full-scale invasion began on Feb. 24, 2022. And, as I told my friend, I was trying to figure out how, after 4 1/2 years of war, we could write about Ukraine in a way that made readers continue to care.
My friend stopped in her tracks. “Over four years of war? That’s someone’s entire high school experience,” she said. One of her sons had recently finished his senior year. “I can’t even imagine.”
Her comment stayed with me as Scott and I discussed how he would approach his assignment.
Scott had proposed going back to find some of the people he had met over the course of the war, to see what had become of them. My friend’s comment made me wonder: Could we write a story about Ukraine looking at the passage of a young person’s life?
We asked Ryan Brown, an editor on our desk who loves narrative journalism, to work with Scott on this idea. Ryan is our Africa editor, but she frequently ventures into magazine stories from around the world and has a gift for bringing people to life on the page and knitting disparate stories around a common thread.
“When Sara told me this story was about coping and what it means to live in a state of seemingly permanent war,” Ryan wrote to Scott before he headed to Ukraine, “the first thing I thought of was children. There are so many young people in Ukraine who either remember nothing before this war or for whom it has been the backdrop to a huge and formative part of their childhoods.”
The statistics are staggering: 2.6 million children are displaced. Some 40% of Ukrainian children ages 3 to 6 do not attend preschool. And perhaps the hardest number of all: 1 in 5 children in Ukraine has lost a relative or friend.
Numbers that large can become difficult to comprehend until you reduce them to individuals.
That’s why Scott went back to visit Olesia Biliaha, an instructor at a community center’s charity arts, dance, and computer program in Izium. Her joy in teaching offers children an escape from a war that has trained them to reflexively head for safety when air-raid sirens sound. He returned to see Yulianna Palahniuk, from Vinnytsia, who learned on her 6th birthday, in May 2022, that her father had been killed in combat. And there was also Serhii Yeroshenko, who was a toddler when his family had to flee their hometown and start anew elsewhere.
The result isn’t light reading.
But I hope you’ll read it. For children, 4 1/2 years can pass relatively quickly. For a child, that length of time can be an entire stage of life.
